title: Job 32:1–5
context: Job 32:1–5 is a prose introduction in the narrator’s voice, kept here as one unit. The three friends stop answering Job “because he was righteous in his own eyes” (32:1), and a new figure appears: Elihu the son of Barachel, the Buzite, of the family of Ram, who has not been mentioned before. Some readers connect Buz with the brother of Uz in Genesis 22:21, though the link is uncertain, and the family of Ram is not otherwise identified. The narrator reports that Elihu’s wrath was kindled against Job “because he justified himself rather than God” (32:2; compare 40:8), and against the three friends “because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job” (32:3). He had waited because they were older (32:4), and he grew angry when they had no answer (32:5). Elihu is not one of the three friends, and the LORD’s later rebuke names Eliphaz and “your two friends” (42:7, 9), not Elihu. How to evaluate Elihu is debated. Some readers see him as preparing the way for the LORD’s speeches in chapters 38–41, some see him as largely repeating the friends with new energy, and others take a position in between, finding real insight mixed with presumption. Some also ask whether the LORD’s opening question, “Who is this who darkens counsel by words without knowledge?” (38:2), glances at Elihu or at Job; readers differ. These notes report what is said and reach no verdict on Elihu’s standing, and they do not treat his speeches as the book’s endorsed doctrine or dismiss them.

verses.text: So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator says the three men stopped answering Job “because he was righteous in his own eyes.” Arminian readers note that this states the friends’ view of Job rather than the book’s verdict on him, since the narrator and the LORD have called Job blameless (1:1, 8; 2:3).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the phrase as describing how Job appeared to the friends, and perhaps how his self-defense sounded. They note that the book holds together Job’s integrity and his need to be humbled before God, and lets the LORD’s speeches address the latter.

verses.text: Then the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel, the Buzite, of the family of Ram, was kindled against Job. His wrath was kindled because he justified himself rather than God.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu’s wrath was kindled against Job “because he justified himself rather than God.” Arminian readers note that Elihu fastens on a real tension in Job’s speeches, his defense of himself at the apparent cost of God’s justice, which the LORD later raises in a question (compare 40:8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same tension and the echo in 40:8. They observe that the narrator reports Elihu’s anger without endorsing or condemning it, and they treat the question of how Job’s integrity and God’s justice fit together as one the whole book answers.

verses.text: Also his wrath was kindled against his three friends, because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu was also angry with the three friends “because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job.” Arminian readers note that Elihu agrees with the reader on one point: the friends condemned Job without proving their case, and their arguments failed to answer his complaints.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu’s criticism of the friends anticipates, in part, the LORD’s later rebuke of the three (42:7). They observe that this does not settle Elihu’s own standing, since he can be right about the friends’ failure while his own answer remains open to evaluation.

verses.text: Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job, because they were older than he.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu had waited to speak because the others were older than he. Arminian readers note the custom of deference to age in the wisdom tradition and see Elihu as respectful at first, though his long silence also seems to have increased the pressure of what he wants to say.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu’s youth is part of how the narrator introduces him, preparing for his claim that understanding does not depend on age. They read the detail neutrally, as setting the scene for a speech whose value readers have assessed in different ways.

verses.text: When Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, his wrath was kindled.
verses.arminianNotes: When Elihu saw no answer in the mouth of the three men, his wrath was kindled. Arminian readers note that the narrator mentions Elihu’s anger four times in this short introduction, and they see the repetition as signaling intensity, which some readers take as zeal and others as rashness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same fourfold mention of anger and hold its significance open. Some take it as righteous indignation at a dishonored God and a mistreated sufferer, others as youthful heat; these notes do not decide between such readings of Elihu’s character.
